title: Why architecture evaluation must change
lead: Classic scenario-based methods assume fixed requirements; agents decide much of their architecture at runtime.
cues: Goals are decomposed into sub-tasks while the agent runs.
The agent makes trade-offs — inside guardrails we design.
Model, prompts and tools change after evaluation.
New scenarios are needed for memory, tools and guardrails.
takeaway: Guardrails become the main architectural control point.

title: AgentArcEval: the process
lead: An ATAM-based method that evaluates agent architecture at design time and keeps re-evaluating at runtime.
cues: Understand first: goals, governance, quality and guardrail requirements, the architecture.
Design time: define and prioritise context scenarios.
Runtime: monitor risks and reprioritise scenarios.
Output: trade-offs, risks, improvements.
takeaway: Agent architecture evaluation never really ends.
source: Lu et al. (2026), AgentArcEval, JSS 232, §4, Fig. 2

title: A quality scenario in six parts
lead: Each scenario follows source → stimulus → environment → artefact → response → measure.
cues: Source and stimulus: who triggers what.
Artefact: the part of the architecture under test.
Environment: the conditions that make it hard.
Measure makes the scenario checkable.
takeaway: A scenario is only useful if its measure can fail.

title: Eleven general scenarios and their measures
lead: The catalogue gives one starter scenario per quality attribute; teams adapt and prioritise them.
cues: Eleven attributes, from accuracy to contestability.
Each comes with a measure a team can track.
Prioritising is where the domain enters.
Luna tax copilot chose 7 of the 11.
takeaway: Prioritising scenarios is where the domain enters the evaluation.

title: Scenarios as a lens on real harnesses
lead: The same scenario catalogue exposes where real harnesses put their architectural effort.
cues: Rows are AgentArcEval attributes; cells are architectural mechanisms.
Pi optimises for a person at a terminal.
Pi Durable optimises for availability.
Hermes invests in safety policy and self-improvement.
takeaway: A scenario catalogue makes the trade-offs between harnesses visible.
source: Lu et al. (2026), AgentArcEval, JSS 232 · our mapping from Barbaste et al. (2026), Harness Engineering, arXiv:2609.00006, Earendil (2026), Pi Durable, earendil.com/posts/pi-durable
